title: Controversy
hook: in the 1230s some banned and burned his books

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guide's last page: know God's ways, then walk in them, with kindness, justice and righteousness. Your line: knowledge leads to kindness. Today, the fights over the man who wrote it.

Open a printed Mishneh Torah to a page of its Book of Knowledge and look at the margins. Next to Maimonides' clean Hebrew sit other voices, in smaller type. Some explain him. Some defend him. A few say, more or less, he's wrong. The book that became a pillar of Jewish learning started out in a fight. In his own lifetime people accused him. After his death, some rabbis banned his philosophical writings, and accounts tell of copies being burned.
screen: `VOICES IN THE MARGIN.` → `ACCUSED, THEN BANNED.` → `WHAT CAME OUT THE OTHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Controversy. First, the accusation. While Maimonides was alive, some readers said his code barely spoke about the resurrection of the dead, and wondered whether he believed in it. He answered with a whole essay: yes, he did, and it already stood in his own list of principles. A man known for clarity had to explain himself. Second, the critic in the margin. A scholar in Provence, Rabbi Abraham ben David, known as the Rabad, wrote sharp notes on the code. Where Maimonides calls anyone who imagines God with a body a heretic, the Rabad objects: greater and better people than that, he writes, held such a view, misled by the plain words of verses. He isn't saying God has a body. He's saying don't call sincere people heretics. Those notes are printed right beside the code. Third, the fire. After Maimonides died, a bitter dispute broke out over his philosophy. Some rabbis feared the Guide and the Book of Knowledge would lead readers away from simple faith, and banned their study. Others defended him just as fiercely. Accounts say his books were burned; historians still argue over exactly who did what. Fourth, then canon. An argument for the sake of heaven, says the Mishnah, will endure, like the arguments of Hillel and Shammai. The banned books stayed on the shelf. His principles went into the prayer book. The critic and the criticized now share a page. Controversy didn't erase him. It became part of how he is read.
screen: `ACCUSED: DID HE DENY RESURRECTION?` · `THE RABAD'S NOTES IN THE MARGIN.` · `BANNED, AND BURNED.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF HEAVEN, IT ENDURES.` · then, large: `CONTROVERSY, THEN CANON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a thinker, writer or teacher you've argued with, out loud or in your head, and keep the disagreement just as it is. Next to it, find one thing that person saw clearly, one sentence of credit. Then picture the two of you on a single page, your note in the margin beside their words, both kept.
Controversy. In Hebrew, machloket. For Maimonides it meant accusation, critique and even burned books, and then a place at the center of Jewish learning. Today's word.
Your line: controversy, then canon. An argument for the sake of heaven lasts. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Printed editions of the Mishneh Torah carry commentaries around the text, including the Rabad's critical notes, so disagreement is part of the page students study.

chat.says: Was Maimonides always this respected, or did people push back on him?
options: They pushed back hard: accusations, critical notes, even bans. Then his work became central.
Never. Every rabbi of his day accepted his code without a single objection.
Only after his death, and the critics finally had his books removed for good.
chat.meaning: He was accused in life, the Rabad critiqued him in the margin, and some banned his books after his death; yet his work stayed at the center.

notes: The index hook dates the bans and burning to the 1230s; under the claims rule the date is left out of the spoken script. Historians usually place the burning in Paris (or Montpellier) around 1232–1233, and its instigators are debated. Please confirm how much the lesson should say.
'accounts tell of copies being burned' and 'historians still argue over exactly who did what' kept deliberately soft. Please confirm.
Essay on Resurrection: the charge that the Mishneh Torah said little about bodily resurrection, and his answer that he affirmed it (it is his 13th principle). Paraphrased; please confirm.

Rabad's gloss on Teshuvah 3:7 paraphrased ('greater and better than he followed this thought, according to what they saw in verses'). Please confirm wording and that the framing (objecting to the label 'heretic', not affirming corporeality) is fair.
Hook: Rabad's glosses are printed in standard editions of the Mishneh Torah; please confirm they appear on Book of Knowledge pages and soften if needed.
'His principles went into the prayer book' refers to Ani Ma'amin and Yigdal, which are based on the thirteen principles; please confirm phrasing.
